name: Cor pulmonale
aliases: right heart failure from lung disease

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / GOLD & ATS guidelines
clinicalPearls: Cor pulmonale is right ventricular enlargement and eventual failure caused by disorders of the lungs, pulmonary vasculature, or ventilation, excluding left heart disease and congenital defects
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the most common underlying cause, with pulmonary hypertension the central intermediary
Symptoms include exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and, as it progresses, ankle swelling and abdominal distension
Signs of right heart failure include raised jugular venous pressure, a left parasternal heave, a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, hepatomegaly, and peripheral oedema
Echocardiography helps assess right ventricular size and function and estimate pulmonary artery pressure, while right heart catheterisation confirms pulmonary hypertension
Treatment is directed primarily at the underlying lung disease and at correcting hypoxaemia, since chronic hypoxia drives pulmonary vasoconstriction
Long-term oxygen therapy in chronically hypoxaemic patients can reduce pulmonary vascular resistance and improve survival
Diuretics can relieve congestion but require caution to avoid reducing preload excessively or worsening metabolic alkalosis
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic lung disease or pulmonary vascular disease raises pulmonary vascular resistance through several mechanisms: alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction, destruction or remodelling of the pulmonary vascular bed reduces its cross-sectional area, and acidosis and polycythaemia further increase resistance. The right ventricle, facing sustained pressure overload, initially hypertrophies to maintain output but ultimately dilates and fails. Rising right-sided filling pressures produce systemic venous congestion, hepatic congestion, and peripheral oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Left ventricular failure causing pulmonary congestion
Right heart failure from congenital heart disease
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to assess right ventricular size and function and estimate pulmonary pressures
Arterial blood gas analysis to detect hypoxaemia and hypercapnia
Electrocardiography for signs of right ventricular strain and right axis deviation
Chest imaging and pulmonary function testing to characterise the underlying lung disease
Right heart catheterisation to confirm and quantify pulmonary hypertension when indicated
redFlags: Rapidly worsening right heart failure with hypotension or syncope
Severe hypoxaemia or hypercapnic respiratory failure
Signs suggesting acute or chronic pulmonary embolism as a cause
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely determined by the severity and reversibility of the underlying pulmonary disorder; the onset of overt right heart failure generally marks advanced disease and portends a poorer outlook, though correcting hypoxaemia and optimising the underlying condition can improve symptoms and survival.
pitfalls: Attributing right heart failure to lung disease without excluding left heart disease or thromboembolism
Failing to correct hypoxaemia, a key reversible driver of pulmonary hypertension
Over-diuresis reducing right ventricular preload and cardiac output
Overlooking treatable causes such as chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
management: Direct treatment at the underlying pulmonary disorder, optimising the primary lung disease such as bronchodilator and inhaled therapy for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Correct chronic hypoxaemia with long-term oxygen therapy to relieve hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
Use diuretics judiciously to relieve peripheral oedema, hepatic congestion and systemic venous overload from right heart failure
Support ventilation, treating hypercapnia and acidosis and considering non-invasive ventilation where hypoventilation contributes
Address contributory factors including smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and management of secondary polycythaemia
Monitor with echocardiography, arterial blood gases and functional assessment to track right ventricular function and pulmonary pressures
Refer to a pulmonary hypertension service for selected patients and escalate as overt right heart failure marks advanced disease
